correction.text: Jammu, the Kashmir Valley, Ladakh, Baltistan and Gilgit town, without the Himachal hills the treaty left to the British

keyframe_review.note: 1846-1847, 169,000 km2: the state made by the Treaty of Amritsar, 'executed on 16 March 1846', which gave Gulab Singh 'all the hilly or mountainous country with its dependencies situated to the eastward of the River Indus' and 'the westward of the River Ravi including Chamba and excluding Lahol' for 75 lakh rupees; the Kashmir Valley had been 'annexed by British East India Company from the Sikhs as war indemnity, on 9 March 1846' (princely state page). Neither page gives an area. Cliopatria's outline holds 68 cells (17,200 km2) of Himachal Pradesh (Lahaul, Spiti, Kullu side) in every year 1846-1884, and its 1947 outline only 7; Article 1 of the Treaty of Amritsar gives Gulab Singh the hill country 'eastward of the River Indus and westward of the River Ravi including Chamba and excluding Lahol', and 'the British kept the territory between the Beas and Ravi, including the Kullu Valley'. Hazara, also handed over, returns to Lahore in early 1847 (ledger). The outline draws no Aksai Chin and none of Hunza, Nagar or Yasin.

1848, 169,500 km2: one cell (253 km2, 73.5 E, 33.3 N) is added on the Poonch side; no page opened dates a frontier change in these years (the 1847 exchange of Hazara for land near Jammu is in the ledger). Unverified: page budget.
1849-1852, 169,000 km2: three cells (759 km2) are removed along a line from Jammu to Gilgit; unverified: page budget.

1853-1858, 164,650 km2: 15 cells (3,800 km2, 74.1-75.2 E, 35.9-36.3 N) are removed: Gilgit. Repair sa-06-d: the Gohar Aman page dates the loss 'in 1852' ('Gohar Aman formed alliance with the Mir of Hunza and led an army into Gilgit Valley in 1852'), so the shape holds from 1852 and the ledger loss is 1852; the Gilgit-Baltistan page gives no year for it. correction.text: the 1853 outline unchanged, but drawn from 1852: the Gohar Aman page has him take Gilgit in 1852, a year before Cliopatria's shape changes

keyframe_review.note: 1859, 164,500 km2: two cells (506 km2) are added along the Jammu-Ladakh line; Gilgit is still out. Unverified: page budget.

keyframe_review.note: 1860-1884, 168,800 km2: Gilgit returns (the same 15 cells): 'It was not until his death in 1860 that Dogras finally managed to subdue Gilgit'. The outline holds 98 of the 101 cells of Baltistan ('By 1840 he had conquered Skardu') and 195 of the 225 of Ladakh. correction.text: the state of 1884 without the Himachal hills, carried through 1885-1890

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1885-1890: Cliopatria has no Kashmir shape from 1885 to 1946; its British Raj outline swallows the state (602 of the 603 cells of the 1884 Kashmir outline lie inside the Raj outline of 1885). The princely state page has the state continue until 'End of British Crown Suzerainty: 15 August 1947', so its 1884 outline (without the Himachal hills) holds until Hunza and Nagar are brought under it in 1891. Cliopatria's outline holds 68 cells (17,200 km2) of Himachal Pradesh (Lahaul, Spiti, Kullu side) in every year 1846-1884, and its 1947 outline only 7; Article 1 of the Treaty of Amritsar gives Gulab Singh the hill country 'eastward of the River Indus and westward of the River Ravi including Chamba and excluding Lahol', and 'the British kept the territory between the Beas and Ravi, including the Kullu Valley'.

correction.text: the Maharaja's dominions in 1891-1946: Jammu, the Kashmir Valley, Ladakh, Baltistan, Gilgit and the northern valleys

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1891-1946: Cliopatria has no Kashmir shape from 1885 to 1946. The Gilgit Agency page: Gilgit, 'Punial, Yasin, Kuh-Ghizar, Ishkoman and Chitral' were 'gradually' brought under the Agency and in 1935 'the Gilgit tehsil of the princely state was leased from the maharaja', who kept his claims; Hunza and Nagar were 'not Kashmir territory, though they are under the suzerainty of Kashmir' (1909 ruling). The state's outline in these years is the 1947 outline (647 cells), which carries the northern valleys; the British administration of Gilgit is the hatched occupation in the ledger. Repair sa-06-d (Yasin Valley page): 'In 1863, Dogras invaded Yasin and massacred its people', but the Kashmir Durbar's governors for 'the Khushwakt districts of Yasin and Kuh' are dated September 1895 (Ghizr added in 1905) and 'In 1895, the British took control of the territory and made it part of the Gilgit Agency'. So of the 25,800 km2 this outline adds to the 1884 shape, Hunza and Nagar come in 1891 (vassal_start) and Yasin, Kuh and the other Ghizer valleys only by 1895; the gazetteer has no name for them, so the outline is drawn whole from 1891 and the four years are a known overdraw.

1947, 182,000 km2 (647 cells): the state at its end, 'End of British Crown Suzerainty: 15 August 1947'; accession to India 'On 26 October 1947' (infobox 27 October). Against the 1884 outline it adds 25,800 km2 in Gilgit-Baltistan (Hunza, Nagar, Yasin, the Ghizer valleys) and drops the Himachal hills (a correction the 1846 and 1860 verdicts make). It carries 11 cells in China (the Shaksgam and Raskam side) and no Aksai Chin, which no page opened mentions. The war page: 'Pakistan had control of one-third of the state' at the ceasefire of 1 January 1949. Repair sa-06-d: the state is carried to the ceasefire of 1 January 1949; Gilgit (1947-11), Azad Kashmir (1947-11) and Baltistan (1948-08) are lost to Pakistan on the ledger and the 1948 keyframe below draws what is left.

correction.text: the state after the first Kashmir war: the 1947 outline without Gilgit, Baltistan and Azad Kashmir, the one-third 'Pakistan had control of' at the ceasefire of 1 January 1949

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1948-1949 (to the ceasefire of 1 January 1949). Gilgit went to Pakistan on 1 November 1947, the western districts after Mirpur fell on 25 November 1947 and Skardu on 14 August 1948; Baltistan is therefore still in the state for the first months of 1948, which the yearly step does not show. The cut is by name, so it follows the present Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, not the ceasefire line itself; the Shaksgam tract and Aksai Chin are not in the 1947 outline.

region.text: Jammu, the Kashmir Valley, Ladakh, Baltistan and the hill country east of the Indus and west of the Ravi

ledger.note: 1846: the state of Jammu and Kashmir is founded. 'Kashmir was sold to the Raja of Jammu, Gulab Singh, for 75 lakh rupees, on 16 March 1846' (infobox 'Foundation of Jammu and Kashmir: 16 March 1846'); the Valley had been 'annexed by British East India Company from the Sikhs as war indemnity, on 9 March 1846' (Treaty of Lahore). The page names the Valley; Jammu, Ladakh and Baltistan come from the Treaty of Amritsar's 'hilly or mountainous country' and Cliopatria's outline.

region.text: Hazara, handed over with the hill country in March 1846

ledger.note: 1846: Hazara goes to Gulab Singh with the rest. The Amritsar page has Hazara 'ceded back to the Lahore Darbar in early 1847, in exchange for territory near Jammu', which implies it came with the 1846 transfer; fighting at the Dub Pass above Garhi Habibullah on 6 January 1847 (Hazara is not in Cliopatria's outline).

region.text: the state of 1846 as the Treaty of Amritsar draws it, the hill country between the Indus and the Ravi without the Himachal hills

ledger.note: 16 March 1846: the new state acknowledges British supremacy. 'Maharajah Gulab Singh acknowledges the supremacy of the British Government' (Treaty of Amritsar, Article 10, done 'the sixteenth day of March' 1846), to be shown by a yearly horse, twelve shawl goats and three pairs of Cashmere shawls; the princely state page calls it 'a subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company from 1846 to 1858'. Recorded from the vassal's side: here the counterpart is the overlord, not the vassal (the overlord's own dossier records the same relation with Kashmir as its vassal). The overlord is named british-empire (the Cliopatria row that sold the state); the east-india-company dossier carries the same relation for the same years, and the orchestrator may substitute that slug.
1847: Hazara returns to Lahore. 'Hazara was later ceded back to the Lahore Darbar in early 1847, in exchange for territory near Jammu' (Amritsar page).

region.text: territory near Jammu: Bhadrawah, Lakhanpur and Chandgraon

ledger.note: 1847: land near Jammu in exchange. Henry Lawrence's mediation of 1847 'left Kashmir with Bhadrawah, Lakhanpur, and Chandgraon, and made Chamba independent of Kashmir'; Captain Abbott fixed the boundary 'west of the Jhelum, along the Kishanganga (Karnah), and then to the Indus'. The page gives no day and no area.

1852: Gilgit is lost. 'Gohar Aman formed alliance with the Mir of Hunza and led an army into Gilgit Valley in 1852', where he defeated the Dogra troops and took Gilgit Fort (Gohar Aman page). The Gilgit-Baltistan page says only 'Gilgit was once again conquered by Gohar Aman' and dates an earlier conquest to 1842, which the Gohar Aman page records as his defeat ('Nathu Shah defeated Gohar Aman at Basin in 1842'); Cliopatria's outline loses the cells a year later, in 1853.

region.text: the state, no longer allied to the Company

ledger.note: 1858: the Company's subsidiary alliance ends with the Company's rule. The page gives 'a subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company from 1846 to 1858' and the state under British paramountcy 'of the British Crown from 1858'; the month (November) is the transfer date the british-empire and british-raj dossiers use, not the page's. Recorded from the vassal's side: here the counterpart is the overlord, not the vassal (the overlord's own dossier records the same relation with Kashmir as its vassal).

region.text: the state, under the paramountcy of the Crown

ledger.note: 1858: the state passes under the paramountcy of the Crown. The page has the state under 'British paramountcy ... of the British Crown from 1858 until British withdrawal'; the month follows the british-raj dossier (its own vassal_start for the state is also November 1858). Recorded from the vassal's side: here the counterpart is the overlord, not the vassal (the overlord's own dossier records the same relation with Kashmir as its vassal).
1860: Gilgit is retaken. 'It was not until his death in 1860 that Dogras finally managed to subdue Gilgit.'

1891: Hunza and Nagar come under Kashmir's suzerainty. 'In 1888, the rulers of Hunza and Nagar expelled Dogras but both states were again subjugated by Anglo-Dogra forces in 1891'; a 1909 ruling holds them 'not Kashmir territory, though they are under the suzerainty of Kashmir', and in 1941 'separate states'.

region.text: the Gilgit Leased Area: 'the part of Gilgit wazarat lying to the west of Indus', leased in 1935

ledger.note: 26 March 1935: the British lease the Gilgit wazarat west of the Indus. 'the Gilgit tehsil of the princely state was leased from the maharaja' (infobox 'Gilgit Wazarat leased: 26 March 1935'); before that the British had 'an Officer on Special Duty ... in 1877 ... till 1882' and 'a permanent Political Agent in 1889', with Gilgit and Astore still 'the Gilgit wazarat of Jammu and Kashmir with its own governor' (dual rule). [Reviewer sa-06-d, 2026-10-25: moved from 1889 to March 1935. The Gilgit Agency page has only a Political Agent from 1889, with Gilgit and Astore still forming 'the Gilgit wazarat of Jammu and Kashmir with its own governor' (dual rule); the land itself passed under the lease, infobox 'Gilgit Wazarat leased: 26 March 1935'. Mirrors british-raj, moved the same way.]

region.text: the Gilgit Agency and leased area

ledger.note: 1947: Gilgit handed back. 'On 1 July 1947, shortly before the partition of India, ... the Gilgit Leased Area [was] retroceded to the Maharaja' (infobox: 30 July 1947); the Gilgit Scouts seized power on 1 November 1947.

region.text: the state, free of British paramountcy

ledger.note: 15 August 1947: British suzerainty over the state ends. Infobox 'End of British Crown Suzerainty: 15 August 1947'; the state then acceded to India on 26 October 1947 (infobox 27 October). Recorded from the vassal's side: here the counterpart is the overlord, not the vassal (the overlord's own dossier records the same relation with Kashmir as its vassal).

region.text: Gilgit and the Agency districts, with Hunza and Nagar

ledger.note: 1 November 1947: Gilgit passes to Pakistan. 'By 1 November, Gilgit-Baltistan had been annexed from the Dogra dynasty' (the Gilgit Scouts 'mutinied and overthrew the governor Ghansara Singh'), five days after the Maharaja's accession to India ('Following the accession of the state to India on 26 October 1947, Indian troops were airlifted to Srinagar'). Mirrors the 1947-11 gain in the islamic-republic-of-pakistan dossier; the state is carried to the ceasefire so that its losses have a mirror.

region.text: Mirpur, Muzaffarabad and Poonch: the western districts Pakistan held at the ceasefire

ledger.note: November 1947: the western districts pass to Pakistan. 'Mirpur was captured by the tribal forces on 25 November 1947'; Muzaffarabad was entered on 22 October and Poonch rose 'at the beginning of October 1947'; the three districts were 'later named Azad Jammu and Kashmir' (no proclamation date on the page, so the region is the present Azad Kashmir). Mirrors the islamic-republic-of-pakistan 1947-11 gain.

1947: Hunza and Nagar accede to Pakistan. 'Hunza acceded to Pakistan on 3 November' and Nagar on '18 November' (Gilgit-Baltistan page), ending the Maharaja's suzerainty. [Reviewer sa-06-d moved this from 1947-11 to 1947-10 because the state then ended in October 1947; the author's repair (2026-10-25) carries the state to the ceasefire of 1 January 1949, so the page's dates (Hunza 3 November, Nagar 18 November 1947) stand again and the month is back to 11.]

14 August 1948: Skardu falls and Baltistan passes to Pakistan. 'On 14 August, Thapa had to surrender Skardu to the Pakistani Army' (the sentence has no year; the Pakistani attack on Skardu 'on 10 February 1948' and the 'year long siege' put it in 1948). Mirrors the islamic-republic-of-pakistan 1948-08 gain.

region.text: the part of the state that stayed with India at the ceasefire: Jammu, the Kashmir Valley and Ladakh

ledger.note: 1 January 1949: the ceasefire divides the state. 'At 23.59 hrs on 1 January 1949, a United Nations-mediated ceasefire came into effect' and 'Pakistan had control of one-third of the state'; the rest, which had acceded to India on 26 October 1947 (infobox 27 October), stays in the Indian Union (princely state page: 'the remaining territory stayed under Indian control'). [Repair sa-06-d, 2026-10-25: this was dated October 1947, the accession; it is moved to the ceasefire so that Pakistan's gains of Gilgit, Azad Kashmir and Baltistan (November 1947 to August 1948) have mirror losses in this ledger. Between the accession and the ceasefire the state's land is in dispute; the war is in wars[] and the pakistan dossier's contest events.]

wars.name: Dogra-Yasin struggle for Gilgit
wars.outcome: Gohar Aman took Gilgit from the Dogras in 1852; he ruled until 1860, and 'Shortly after his death Dogras recaptured Gilgit from his son' (Gohar Aman page; Gilgit-Baltistan page: 'It was not until his death in 1860 that Dogras finally managed to subdue Gilgit').
wars.note: Start 1852 from the Gohar Aman page ('led an army into Gilgit Valley in 1852'); the recapture year (1860) is the Gilgit-Baltistan page's, since the Gohar Aman page gives no year for it. The Gilgit-Baltistan page's 1842 conquest is a defeat on the Gohar Aman page.

wars.name: Hunza-Nagar Campaign
wars.outcome: Hunza and Nagar 'again subjugated by Anglo-Dogra forces in 1891'.
wars.note: The rulers had expelled the Dogras in 1888.

wars.name: Indo-Pakistani War of 1947-1948

zones.text: the whole state, divided by the ceasefire line

wars.outcome: Accession to India on 26 October 1947; Gilgit mutiny on 1 November; Mirpur taken on 25 November 1947; ceasefire at 23.59 hrs on 1 January 1949 with Pakistan holding one-third of the state.
wars.note: Poonch rebelled in October 1947; Skardu fell in August 1948. [Repair sa-06-d, 2026-10-25: the reviewer had cut 'to' from 1949 to 1947 because the state ended in 1947-10; the state is now carried to the ceasefire (identity.end 1949-01), so the war runs 1947-1949 inside its life again.]

certainty.note: The Treaty of Amritsar draws the state as the hill country between the Indus and the Ravi, and Captain Abbott's 1847 commission fixed only the line west of the Jhelum and along the Kishanganga; the Karakoram, Aksai Chin and Chinese frontiers were never fixed, and the Hunza and Nagar border was not a boundary of the state. From the accession of 26 October 1947 to the ceasefire of 1 January 1949 the state's line is a front, not a frontier; the ceasefire line itself was never fixed on the ground by treaty.

notes:
Written by sa-06-d from six pages (budget up to 5; the war page and the Gilgit Agency page are shared with the pakistan and british-raj dossiers). CLIOPATRIA ROW: 'Kashmir and Jammu' has shapes only for 1846-1884 and 1947. For 1885-1946 the state does not exist in Cliopatria: the British Raj outline of 1885 swallows its 1884 shape (602 of 603 cells) and the Raj shape runs to 1946; two new keyframes (1885-1890, 1891-1946) restore it and the british-raj dossier subtracts the 1947 Kashmir outline from its own corrections. Cliopatria's 1846-1884 outline carries 17,200 km2 of Himachal Pradesh (Lahaul, Spiti, Kullu side) which the Treaty of Amritsar excluded ('excluding Lahol'); corrected in the 1846 and 1860 verdicts. The 1947 outline has no Aksai Chin (about 37,000 km2, claimed by the state) and 11 cells in China. NOT RESOLVED: the pages give no area for the state; the loss of Gilgit in 1852-1853 (page undated); the 1848-1849 and 1859 cell changes (unverified: page budget); Poonch's semi-autonomous jagir; the Sino-Tibetan frontier of Ladakh (Chushul 1842, the Johnson Line 1865, the 1899 Macartney-MacDonald line: none on the pages opened); the years of Baltistan's and Gilgit's Dogra conquest (the Gilgit-Baltistan page gives Baltistan 1840 and Gilgit 1842 for Gohar Aman, not for the Dogras); the 1935 lease's term; the Standstill Agreement of 1947 (page silent); the reigns of the Maharajas after Gulab Singh (1846-1857) and before Hari Singh (1925-1947): the princely state page gives only the first and last, so no ruler strip. PAGE CONFLICTS: accession 26 October 1947 in the text and 27 October in the infobox; the Gilgit retrocession 1 July in the text and 30 July in the infobox. COUNTERPARTS WITHOUT A DOSSIER: hunza-and-nagar, 'Yasin (Gohar Aman)'. The sikh-empire dossier names british-empire (not this state) as the taker of Kashmir in 1846, which agrees with the founding event here.

REPAIR 2026-10-25 (review fail): (1) four vassal-side events added for the British overlordship (1846-03 and 1858-11 british-empire; 1858-11 and 1947-08 british-raj; the east-india-company dossier carries the same relation, so the slug may be swapped by the orchestrator); they are written with the overlord as counterpart, the reverse of the schema's overlord-side vassal_start, and say so in their notes. (2) The state is carried from the accession (1947-10) to the ceasefire of 1 January 1949 (identity.end, dissolve, war, certainty, capitals, one new keyframe) and gains loss events to islamic-republic-of-pakistan for Gilgit (1947-11), Azad Kashmir (1947-11) and Baltistan (1948-08), mirroring the pakistan dossier, which was not touched (verdict thin); the alternative (end 1947-10 and republic-of-india as the counterpart of pakistan's gains) would have needed an edit there. The Hunza-Nagar vassal_end is back at 1947-11. (3) Gilgit's loss to Gohar Aman is 1852 (Gohar Aman page), no longer 1853 at confidence 1; the Gilgit-Baltistan page's '1842' conquest is a defeat on the Gohar Aman page. (4) Yasin: invasion 1863, Kashmir governors 1895 (Yasin Valley page); not drawn as an event, noted in the 1891 keyframe. NOT FIXED: 1848, 1849 and 1859 cell changes (page budget, allowed).
